description:
We are a team of computer science students passionate about using technology to address real-world environmental challenges.

We aim to combine software development, data analysis, and visualization to make satellite-based fire information more accessible and useful.
summary:
We developed a web application that challenges users to predict how a wildfire will spread, then invites them to explore historical wildfire patterns through integrated MODIS and VIIRS data. An interactive simulation captures users’ interest and makes the difficulty of wildfire prediction tangible by asking them to anticipate a fire’s next move.
Although decades of satellite observations exist, differences in spatial resolution, observation timing, and detection sensitivity make these datasets difficult to combine and compare across years. To address this, we designed a common fire intensity index that uses MODIS as a reference while incorporating VIIRS’s finer spatial information and additional detections.
Our website transforms these integrated observations into accessible visualizations of historical wildfire events, their development over time, and seasonal and long-term patterns. Users can move from attempting a prediction themselves to examining how actual fires unfolded. By connecting an engaging simulation with historical data exploration, the project makes wildfire information easier to understand and highlights the value of harmonized satellite records for studying wildfire behavior and supporting future prediction research.
details:
We harmonized the data from MODIS and VIIRS. Based on this data, we developed a web application that shows the long-term patterns of wildfires in a selected region and time period while letting users experience firsthand how difficult it is to predict fires without past data.

How our web works: factors we considered

We analyzed the data provided by MODIS and VIIRS. MODIS provides a long-term record for tracking wildfire trends while VIIRS offers finer spatial detail that helps detect smaller fires and map fire boundaries more precisely. Therefore, combining these data helps to more effectively represent wildfire states. However, the difference of pixels, time and position makes it hard to compare them directly. Also, we can’t simply add those data to get an integrated indicator.

We developed a 500 m fire intensity index that uses MODIS FRP as its reference while incorporating VIIRS’s finer spatial information. The method preserves MODIS FRP totals during redistribution and limits repeated counting across VIIRS platforms.

First, each satellite pixel’s footprint was approximated as a rectangle using its center coordinates and reported scan and track dimensions. FRP was then distributed onto a common 500 m × 500 m grid according to the overlapping area, preserving each pixel’s total FRP.

To account for differences between sensors, we compared MODIS and VIIRS observations recorded in the same UTC minute over the overlap of their approximated pixel footprints. A separate 1 km calibration grid organized these comparisons. Relative scale coefficients were estimated separately for each VIIRS platform and day/night category using a robust method that reduces the influence of extreme ratios. VIIRS FRP was converted to the MODIS reference scale by dividing it by the corresponding coefficient.

VIIRS contributes to the integrated index in two ways. First, it refines the spatial distribution within MODIS footprints. Some of the MODIS FRP initially allocated outside VIIRS-supported areas is transferred into supported areas. The transferred amount follows the average normalized spatial pattern of the contributing VIIRS platforms. This redistribution preserves the MODIS total. The redistribution ratio is set to 0.5, which considers information from MODIS and VIIRS together.

Second, VIIRS detections outside MODIS-detected footprints are added as potential fires missed by MODIS. Their FRP is converted to the MODIS reference scale, and contributions from multiple VIIRS platforms are averaged within connected footprint groups to limit repeated counting. Only the portions outside MODIS footprints are added.

The final index combines the redistributed MODIS contribution with the additional VIIRS contribution. Historical periods without VIIRS use MODIS alone. When MODIS is unavailable, VIIRS can use coefficients learned during the overlap period, provided those relationships remain applicable. Observations without reliable coefficients retain missing calibrated values rather than being treated as zero.

This approach supports consistent mapping and comparison while acknowledging that approximate footprints and minute-level timestamps do not guarantee perfectly matched observations.

We then adapted the spatiotemporal clustering approach described by McClure et al. (2023) to identify individual fire events. Spatially neighboring detections were grouped at each observation time to create fire snapshots, which were then linked across time based on spatial and temporal proximity. We applied this approach to our integrated fire intensity observations for California from 2006 to 2026, assigning a unique event id to each resulting fire event.

Using this harmonized dataset, we visualized three key metrics over time: average Fire Radiative Power (FRP), fire duration per event, and burned area (measured by grid cells per event).

Because fire sizes vary drastically, we separated events into small, large, extreme, and total categories so that catastrophic megafires wouldn't skew the averages of typical fires.

To highlight seasonal trends, we averaged these metrics week by week across the year (weeks 1–52). On each graph, we plotted 4-year historical averages alongside the current data for 2026. This allows users to easily see whether recent wildfire activity aligns with historical baselines or signals shifting, more severe patterns.

For short-term patterns, users can select a specific date to view heatmaps showing FRP values across three time windows: two weeks (±7 days), two months (±1 month), and the full selected year.

Finally, to show spatial patterns, we display fire activity directly on an interactive regional map, color-coded by FRP intensity. By tracking active burning over a 15-day window (±7 days from the selected date), users can intuitively watch how a wildfire spreads and moves over time.

Creativity

To make the complex challenge of fire forecasting intuitive and engaging, we designed an interactive, game-like simulation. Users are given real-time environmental conditions—such as wind direction, humidity, and terrain—and must predict which way an active fire will spread without access to historical patterns. After submitting their prediction, users receive an accuracy score based on the cosine of the directional error angle between their guess and the actual observed fire spread. This hands-on challenge proves that even with immediate weather and environmental data in hand, predicting wildfire behavior remains remarkably difficult without long-term satellite baselines.

Furthermore, we replaced rigid administrative borders with flexible spatial exploration. Users have full freedom to define any custom region of interest by dragging bounding boxes or entering specific coordinates. This dynamic interface allows users to isolate and analyze wildfire patterns across any custom geographic scale.

Benefits

First, our application helps everyday users understand why satellite data is crucial for wildfire prediction. By experiencing the difficulty of forecasting fire spread firsthand, users quickly grasp why historical baselines matter. Interactive features like regional and timeline filters let them explore the data directly, turning complex satellite observations into intuitive learning. 

Second, it bridges the technical gap between MODIS and VIIRS by providing harmonized long-term visualizations. The incompatibility between these sensors typically makes decades-long cross comparison labor intensive. By unifying them into a continuous record, our platform saves users significant time and allows anyone, regardless of technical background, to easily explore long-term burning trends.

Intended Impact

With this project, we intend to raise awareness of the importance of satellite data in dealing with the ongoing problem of wildfires while also providing accessible insights into 20-year burning activity trends. 

Tools

Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript 

Data Processing: Python
